paragraphs: “And Alyosha? What about his opinion, the one you were so desperate to hear?” cried Madame Hohlakov. Her voice was sarcastic and angry.

“I haven’t forgotten it,” cried Katerina Ivanovna, stopping short. “Why must you be so hostile at a moment like this?” she added, with warm and bitter reproach. “What I said, I say again. I have to have his opinion. More than that, I have to have his decision! Whatever he says is what will be done. You can see how I long to hear you, Alexey Fyodorovitch.... But what’s the matter?”
“I wouldn’t have believed it. I just don’t understand it!” Alyosha cried suddenly, in distress.
“What? What?”

“He’s going to Moscow, and you cry out that you’re glad. You said it on purpose! Then you start explaining that you’re not glad about that, only sorry—sorry to be losing a friend. But that was acting too—you were playing a part—as if you were on a stage!”
“On a stage? What? What are you saying?” exclaimed Katerina Ivanovna, deeply astonished, flushing crimson and frowning.
“You tell him you’re sorry to lose a friend, and yet you keep telling him to his face how lucky it is that he’s leaving,” said Alyosha breathlessly. He was standing at the table and had not sat down.
“What are you talking about? I don’t understand.”

“I don’t understand it myself.... It was as if I saw something in a flash ... I know I’m not saying it right, but I’ll say it anyway,” Alyosha went on in the same shaking, broken voice. “What I see is that maybe you don’t love Dmitri at all ... and never have, right from the start.... And Dmitri has never loved you either ... he only respects you.... I truly don’t know how I dare say all this, but somebody has to tell the truth ... because nobody here will.”
“What truth?” cried Katerina Ivanovna, with a hysterical edge in her voice.

“I’ll tell you,” Alyosha went on, in desperate haste, as if he were leaping off a rooftop. “Call Dmitri; I’ll go and get him—let him come here, take your hand, take Ivan’s, and join your hands together. Because you’re torturing Ivan, simply because you love him—and you torture him because you love Dmitri out of ‘self-laceration’—with an unreal love—because you’ve talked yourself into it.”
Alyosha stopped short and said nothing more.
“You ... you ... you’re a little religious idiot—that’s what you are!” Katerina Ivanovna snapped. Her face had gone white, and her lips shook with anger.
Ivan suddenly laughed and got to his feet. His hat was in his hand.

“You’re wrong, my good Alyosha,” he said, with a look on his face that Alyosha had never seen there—a look of youthful sincerity and strong, openly frank feeling. “Katerina Ivanovna has never cared for me! All along she has known that I cared for her—though I never said one word to her about my love—she knew, but she didn’t care for me. And I was never her friend either, not for a moment; she’s too proud to need my friendship. She kept me beside her as a means of revenge. Through me, and against me, she paid back every insult she has had from Dmitri since the day they met. Even that first meeting has festered in her heart as an insult—that’s the kind of heart she has! She has talked to me about nothing but her love for him. I’m going now; but believe me, Katerina Ivanovna, you really do love him. And the more he insults you, the more you love him—that’s your ‘laceration.’ You love him as he is; you love him for insulting you. If he reformed, you’d drop him at once and stop loving him. But you need him, so that you can go on admiring your own heroic faithfulness and reproaching him for his unfaithfulness. And all of it comes from pride. Oh, there’s plenty of humiliation and self-abasement in it, but it all comes from pride.... I’m too young, and I’ve loved you too much. I know I shouldn’t say this; it would be more dignified of me just to leave, and less insulting to you. But I’m going far away, and I’ll never come back.... It’s for ever. I don’t want to sit beside a ‘laceration.’... But I don’t know how to speak now. I’ve said everything.... Good-by, Katerina Ivanovna; you can’t be angry with me, since I’m punished a hundred times worse than you, if only because I’ll never see you again. Good-by! I don’t want your hand. You’ve tortured me too deliberately for me to forgive you at this moment. I’ll forgive you later, but right now I don’t want your hand. ‘Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht,’” he added, with a forced smile, showing, however, that he could read Schiller, and had read him till he knew him by heart—which Alyosha would never have believed. He walked out without saying good-by even to his hostess, Madame Hohlakov. Alyosha clasped his hands.

“Ivan!” he cried desperately after him. “Come back, Ivan! No, nothing will bring him back now!” he cried again, realizing it with regret. “But it’s my fault, my fault! I started it! Ivan spoke in anger, and he was wrong. Unfair, and angry. He has to come back, he has to come back here,” Alyosha kept exclaiming, beside himself.
Katerina Ivanovna suddenly went off into the next room.
“You haven’t done any harm. You were wonderful, like an angel,” Madame Hohlakov whispered quickly and ecstatically to Alyosha. “I’ll do all I can to keep Ivan Fyodorovitch from leaving.”
Her face was shining with delight, which distressed Alyosha greatly, but Katerina Ivanovna suddenly came back. She had two hundred-rouble notes in her hand.

“I have a great favor to ask you, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she began, speaking to Alyosha in a voice that sounded calm and even, as though nothing had happened. “A week ago—yes, I think it was a week—Dmitri Fyodorovitch did something hasty and unjust—something very ugly. There’s a low tavern here, and in it he came across that discharged officer, that captain, whom your father used to employ in some business. Dmitri Fyodorovitch lost his temper with this captain over something, grabbed him by the beard and dragged him out into the street, and for some distance along it, in that insulting way. And I’m told that the captain’s son, a boy, hardly more than a child, who goes to school here, saw it and ran along beside them crying and begging for his father, appealing to everyone to defend him, while everyone laughed. You must forgive me, Alexey Fyodorovitch, but I can’t think of that disgraceful act of _his_ without indignation ... one of those acts only Dmitri Fyodorovitch could commit in his anger ... and in his passions! I can’t even describe it.... I can’t find the words. I’ve asked about his victim, and I find he’s a very poor man. His name is Snegiryov. He did something wrong in the army and was discharged. I can’t tell you what. Now he has sunk into terrible poverty, with his family—an unhappy family of sick children and, I believe, an insane wife. He has lived here a long time; he used to work as a copying clerk, but now he gets no work at all. I thought that if you ... that is, I thought ... I don’t know. I’m so muddled. You see, I wanted to ask you, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, to go to him, to find some excuse to call on them—I mean on that captain—oh, goodness, how badly I explain it!—and gently, carefully, the way only you can” (Alyosha blushed), “to manage to give him this help, these two hundred roubles. He’ll be sure to take it.... I mean, persuade him to take it.... Or rather, what do I mean? You see, it’s not meant as payment to stop him from going to law (because I believe he meant to), but simply as a sign of sympathy, a wish to help him, from me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s betrothed, not from himself.... But you understand.... I’d go myself, but you’ll do it so much better. He lives in Lake Street, in the house of a woman called Kalmikov.... For God’s sake, Alexey Fyodorovitch, do this for me, and now ... now I’m rather ... tired. Good-by!”

She turned and vanished behind the portière so fast that Alyosha had no time to say a word, though he wanted to. He longed to beg her pardon, to blame himself, to say something, for his heart was full and he couldn’t bear to leave the room without saying it. But Madame Hohlakov took him by the hand and led him away with her. In the hall she stopped him again, as before.

“She’s proud, she’s fighting with herself; but she’s kind, charming, generous,” she exclaimed in a half-whisper. “Oh, how I love her, especially at times, and how glad I am about everything again! Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, you didn’t know, but I must tell you, that all of us, all—her two aunts, I, everyone, even Lise—have for the last month been hoping and praying for one thing only: that she would give up your favorite Dmitri, who pays her no attention and doesn’t care for her, and marry Ivan Fyodorovitch—such an excellent, cultivated young man, who loves her more than anything in the world. We’re in a regular plot to bring it about, and I’m even staying on here, maybe, for that very reason.”
“But she was crying—she’s been hurt again,” cried Alyosha.
“Don’t ever trust a woman’s tears, Alexey Fyodorovitch. In cases like this I’m never for the women. I’m always on the men’s side.”
“Mamma, you’re spoiling him,” Lise’s little voice called from behind the door.
“No, it was all my fault. I’m horribly to blame,” Alyosha repeated, inconsolable, hiding his face in his hands in an agony of remorse for his thoughtlessness.
“Not at all, quite the reverse; you were an angel, an angel. I’m ready to say so a thousand times over.”
“Mamma, how was he an angel?” Lise’s voice was heard again.
“I got the idea all at once,” Alyosha went on, as though he hadn’t heard Lise, “that she loved Ivan, and so I said that stupid thing.... What will happen now?”
“To who, to who?” cried Lise. “Mamma, you really want to kill me. I’m asking you and you won’t answer.”
Just then the maid ran in.
“Katerina Ivanovna is ill.... She’s crying, struggling ... hysterics.”
“What is it?” cried Lise, in a tone of real alarm. “Mamma, I’ll be the one having hysterics, not her!”

“Lise, for mercy’s sake, don’t scream, don’t hound me. At your age you can’t know everything grown-up people know. I’ll come and tell you whatever you ought to know. Oh, mercy on us! I’m coming, I’m coming.... Hysterics is a good sign, Alexey Fyodorovitch; it’s excellent that she’s hysterical. That’s exactly as it should be. In cases like this I’m always against the woman, against all these feminine tears and hysterics. Run and tell her, Yulia, that I’ll fly to her. As for Ivan Fyodorovitch leaving like that, it’s her own fault. But he won’t leave. Lise, for mercy’s sake, don’t scream! Oh, yes; you’re not screaming. It’s I who am screaming. Forgive your mamma; but I’m delighted, delighted, delighted! Did you notice, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how young, how young Ivan Fyodorovitch looked just now when he went out, when he said all that and went out? I thought he was so learned, such a _savant_, and all of a sudden he was so warm, so open and youthful, with such youthful inexperience, and it was all so fine, just like you.... And the way he recited that German verse, it was exactly like you! But I must fly, I must fly! Alexey Fyodorovitch, hurry and do what she asked, and then hurry back. Lise, do you want anything now? For mercy’s sake, don’t keep Alexey Fyodorovitch even a minute. He’ll come straight back to you.”
Madame Hohlakov finally ran off. Before leaving, Alyosha was about to open the door to see Lise.
“Don’t you dare,” cried Lise. “Not now, not on any account. Talk through the door. How did you come to be an angel? That’s the one thing I want to know.”
“For a terrible piece of stupidity, Lise! Good-by!”
“Don’t you dare leave like that!” Lise began.
“Lise, I have a real sorrow! I’ll be back in a moment, but I have a great, great sorrow!”
And he ran out of the room.
